name: Zenagamtide
lead: Zenagamtide, better known by the name amycretin, is an investigational once-weekly injectable and daily oral drug from Novo Nordisk that activates both the GLP-1 and amylin receptors within a single peptide molecule.[1][3] It is being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes and is not approved.[1][2]

For appearance, the interest lies in fat loss: GLP-1-class drugs reduce appetite, and substantial loss of body fat changes facial fullness, jawline definition and overall body composition, which is why incretin drugs are widely discussed in physique and looks communities. Amycretin is of interest because its early-trial weight reductions were reported to be large and its tablet form is unusual for the class.[1][2][3]

In a phase 1b/2a trial of 125 adults with overweight or obesity running up to 36 weeks, subcutaneous amycretin was studied for safety, tolerability and weight effects.[1][3] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a mean weight loss of 24.3 percent at the 60 mg weekly dose and gastrointestinal adverse events as the most common effects.[2] Phase 3 programs were reported to be planned or starting.[2] The compound has since received the nonproprietary name zenagamtide, and phase 2 trials in type 2 diabetes have been published in the Lancet.[9][10]

paras: GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide set new benchmarks for medicines treating type 2 diabetes and obesity, and next-generation agents that engage additional hormone receptors are advancing rapidly, according to a 2026 Endocrine Reviews article.[11] Amylin analogues have been described as a possible next major class of weight-loss therapy, with reviews covering experimental data and early-phase trials.[12][13] Amycretin was developed as a single molecule carrying both activities, rather than a co-administered pair of drugs.[1][2]

Amycretin is a single peptide that combines GLP-1-like and amylin-like activity. GLP-1 receptor activation affects appetite, while amylin activity is described as affecting satiety and gastric emptying.[1][2] In rodent studies amycretin was reported to reduce body weight and improve metabolic dysfunction.[5]

Grokipedia describes a 68-amino-acid peptide with a C18 diacid modification for albumin binding and reports a half-life of about 4 days for the injectable form.[2] The oral form uses the absorption enhancer salcaprozate sodium.[1]

Grokipedia reports that gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were the most frequent, mostly mild to moderate, with injection-site reactions and some cases of dysesthesia in the injectable trial.[2]

A first-in-human phase 1 trial evaluated safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of single and multiple ascending doses.[4] A phase 1b/2a randomised placebo-controlled trial studied subcutaneous amycretin for up to 36 weeks in 125 participants with overweight or obesity.[3] Grokipedia reports 24.3 percent mean weight loss at 36 weeks in the 60 mg group, with placebo groups changing by between a 1.1 percent loss and a 2.0 percent gain, and says weight had not plateaued, but this is an AI-generated source.[2]

Wikipedia dates the oral phase 1 announcement to 7 March 2024 and the subcutaneous phase 1b/2a announcement to January 2025.[1] Grokipedia reports 13.1 percent weight loss at 12 weeks for the oral form in phase 1 and an HbA1c reduction of 1.5 percent in a 36-week oral type 2 diabetes trial.[2] In 2026 the Lancet published phase 2 trials of once-weekly subcutaneous and once-daily oral zenagamtide in type 2 diabetes.[9][10] A phase 1 study of oral amycretin in Japanese men with obesity (36 participants, started September 2023) has been completed,[6] and a phase 1 study examined the effect of renal impairment on pharmacokinetics, safety and tolerability.[15] Commentary in the Lancet and reviews discuss the dual-agonist approach.[7][8]
Novo Nordisk announced phase 1 oral results in March 2024 and phase 1b/2a subcutaneous results in January 2025.[1] Grokipedia reports the oral form moved to phase 3 in 2025.[2]

Wikipedia reports that Novo Nordisk's chief executive at the time expected amycretin to launch mostly as an injectable at first, with oral versions later in higher-priced markets.[1] Amycretin is discussed in obesity-medicine coverage and reviews as one of several multi-receptor candidates, alongside other incretin-based medicines.[11][14] Because it is not approved, it is not sold as a prescription product.

In rodents, amycretin was reported to reduce body weight and improve metabolic dysfunction.[5] Reviews of incretin-based therapies discuss how engaging amylin receptors alongside GLP-1 could increase weight loss compared with single-hormone drugs, and a 2026 Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology review examined multisystem benefits of obesity medications more broadly.[11][16] Trials in participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes are the main route to approval, with phase 3 programmes described as starting.[2]

card.summary: Novo Nordisk's investigational GLP-1 plus amylin dual agonist, with large weight-loss figures in early trials and no approval yet.
card.note: Not approved; reported gastrointestinal side effects.

quick.overview:
Zenagamtide is the name for amycretin, a single molecule that activates GLP-1 and amylin receptors. Novo Nordisk is developing weekly injectable and daily oral forms for obesity and diabetes.

Early trials were published in the Lancet in 2025; an AI-generated source reports up to about 24 percent weight loss at 36 weeks in the injectable trial.
quick.mechanism: It combines GLP-1 and amylin receptor activity in one peptide, acting on appetite, satiety and gastric emptying.
quick.risks: Gastrointestinal effects were the most common reported adverse events. It is investigational and not approved.

chain: Single peptide activates GLP-1 and amylin receptors
Reduced energy intake and weight loss, changing body and facial fat
angle.text: Zenagamtide is being tested as a weight-loss medicine; people interested in leaner body and facial contours follow it as a possible successor to semaglutide-type drugs. It is not available outside clinical trials.
